answer:
The bubble-point pressure is about **96.3 kPa** (0.963 bar, about 722 mmHg). It is not the Raoult's-law average.

**Why it's not Raoult's law:** water and n-hexane are almost completely immiscible. A 50/50 liquid at 60 °C splits into two nearly pure liquid layers, one water and one hexane. Each layer exerts its own full vapour pressure, so at the bubble point:

P_bubble = P_sat(water) + P_sat(n-hexane)

This holds for any overall composition where both liquid layers are present, so the 50/50 split does not change the answer.

**Values at 60 °C (333.15 K), calculated:**

| | Antoine (NIST) | CoolProp |
|---|---|---|
| P_sat water | 19.93 kPa | 19.95 kPa |
| P_sat n-hexane | 76.36 kPa | 76.41 kPa |
| **Bubble-point pressure** | **96.29 kPa** | **96.36 kPa** |

The Antoine water value also matches the Buck correlation (19.945 kPa).

**First vapour composition:** about 79.3 mol% hexane and 20.7 mol% water. That comes from 76.4/96.3 for hexane.

**Common wrong answer:** treating the mixture as ideal (Raoult's law) gives 0.5·19.9 + 0.5·76.4 ≈ 48.1 kPa. That is roughly half the real value, because it ignores the phase split.

**Not checked:** I assumed the two liquids are fully immiscible. I did not calculate the small mutual solubilities; they are expected to lower the result by much less than 1%. I made no files.
